prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds. Its greedy policy chooses DONE before any placement in 100% of episodes. The likely cause is that it can't see far enough. Placements land at the left-right mirror (column 8 - dx - x), but two 3x3 layers on top of 1x1 layers give each placement score only a 5x5 view. So the score for a placement can't see the target cells near the mirrored column, which can be up to 7 columns away. Random placements mostly fill wrong cells and lose reward, so the agent learns to choose DONE. Any network that improves must learn a mapping that spans the whole grid, at least from column x to its mirror. This round tests two learned ways to do that: weights shared along each row and column, and attention over all cells with learned position codes. The third candidate tests whether more PPO updates help on this small budget. None flips the grid by hand, so the idea should carry over to other worlds.

### Round 2
All four trials so far scored 0. The common failure is the policy collapsing to DONE. Early in training, random placements earn negative returns (about -2 over an episode) while DONE earns 0. So DONE wins unless good placements become learnable quickly. Placing well is hard here because of the mirror rule: a brick chosen at column x lands at column 8-dx-x, so local conv features at the anchor describe the wrong cells. Only the axis-mixing net (seed 0) recovered, and it placed very accurately (0.03 cells outside the target per episode, IoU 0.44). It still stopped after about 6 placements, and its episodes were still getting longer when training ended (length 8.0). This suggests two things: global row mixing let it learn the mirror, and its main remaining weakness was not enough training plus DONE coming too early. Next, give the head direct access to features flipped left-to-right after a learned layer, so the footprint pooling at an anchor sees the cells where the brick really lands. Then test more samples, and a DONE head that knows how good the best placement is.

### Round 3
Round 1 networks could not see where a brick actually lands, and all scored 0. Concatenating the left-right flipped features before the footprint pooling head lined the head up with the real landing cells. That took dev success from 0 to 0.53. A DONE head that also sees the detached max and logsumexp of the placement logits raised it to 0.68 (seeds 0.79 and 0.57). The gap between seeds is about 0.2, so differences of 0.15 or less are noise. Two epochs with more samples (r2c2) gave 0.46, with seeds 0.17 and 0.76. That is no better and probably no worse. In r2c3, training success was still rising at the end of the budget (0.35, then 0.63), with high IoU (0.97) and few wrong cells. The remaining failures are occasional wrong or misordered placements and too little training. Next I refine r2c3 three ways: more updates on the same samples, a more expressive footprint head, and a longer horizon so the exact-build bonus counts for more.

### Round 4
Two things matter most. First, the policy head must pool over the flipped features (mirror-concat), so it scores the cells where a brick will really land. Second, the DONE head should see the detached placement logits. Halving n_envs to 128 (r3c1) lifted dev success from 0.68 to 0.88, with both seeds close together. r2c3 and r3c1 both took 3,712 gradient steps with 128-sample minibatches. So the gain came from collecting data with a more recent policy, not from more optimisation. The training curve for r3c1 levels off at about 0.85 from 75% of training onward. A footprint-shaped convolution in the head (r3c2) did worse. Gamma 0.99 (r3c3) also did worse. 2 epochs (r2c2) was mixed and noisy. For the last round, all three candidates keep the r3c1 network and push further along the axis that worked. One halves n_envs again to 64. One uses 3 epochs, which buys more samples and updates. One combines both changes to give the best chance at the final result.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c1 + 3 epochs (more samples)
hypothesis: r3c1's network and 128 worlds, with 3 PPO epochs instead of 4. The budget then gives about 1.3x more samples (about 159k steps) and about 78 updates instead of 58. r3c1's training success leveled off near 0.85 late in training, so more fresh data may help more than a fourth pass over old data. Refuted if dev success falls below 0.83.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 states the rule outright: "Placements land at the left-right mirror (column 8 - dx - x)". Both name the change (a left-right mirror of the landing column) and give the exact formula from the hidden rule.
